 Lessons from Haze: Your Money is in the Air We Breathe
 Adam Azlan 
 November 5, 2026 
 • 
 4 min read
 • 
 0 Comments 
 Share on Whatsapp 
 Share on Facebook

 Share via Email 
 Share on Bluesky 
 Add as a preferred source on Google 
 If the evidence confirms the companies behind the haze-causing fires, the next question is who is funding them. The trail may lead to our own savings, retirement funds, and banks. 
 Skip to our Key Demands 
 What we breathe
 This haze season, air quality across our region reached life-threatening levels that closed schools, emptied streets, and cleared out aisles of facemasks. Each country uses its own index, where above 150 is unhealthy and above 300 is hazardous for all:
 Malaysia (API): Serian in Sarawak hit 521 on 4 September , and Klang and Kuala Lumpur were still at 163 and 166 on 30 September .
 Singapore (PSI): central Singapore reached 191 on 9 October , the highest of the season so far.
 Indonesia (ISPU): the index in Central Kalimantan exceeded 1,200 on 14 October , four times the hazardous level.
 The cost
 On the economy: A report commissioned by the Federation of Malaysian Manufacturers estimates the haze cost Malaysia RM8 billion in welfare losses . 
 Our health: The same report links the haze to about 1,700 premature deaths in Malaysia. The Health Ministry recorded asthma cases up 259% and upper respiratory infections up 124% .
 Indonesia: The haze this year has been linked to more than 4,390 extra hospitalisations and at least 635,000 severe asthma attacks among children .
 Who is linked to the fires
 On 5 October, Greenpeace and Pantau Gambut named the top 20 entities linked to haze source points in Indonesia. The list includes Malaysian plantation group Kuala Lumpur Kepong, through its link to an Indonesian entity PT MJSP, and concessions tied to Singapore-based groups. They have since provided a statement , despite the Indonesian government not yet releasing the full list of companies involved.
 Indonesian authorities have said they are investigating 19 companies but have not named them. That’s why we and our civil society allies have asked Indonesia to publish the list , so that Malaysia may investigate any Malaysian-linked companies and hold them to account.
 Singapore is already acting
 Singapore’s National Environment Agency has issued legal notices to 10 companies in Indonesia under its Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, requiring them to put out fires and submit prevention plans. It then issued notices to 10 Singapore-registered palm oil and forestry companies , asking about their concessions and corporate links. On 28 October, the Singapore government met executives from those 10 companies , and Singapore is now looking to strengthen the law further . The notices are not findings of legal responsibility, but they show what a government can do when it asks for the evidence. The Monetary Authority of Singapore has also instructed its banks to check their financing and ensure that strong measures are taken against burning practices and to ensure prevention of fires. In Malaysia, civil society has been urging Parliament to expedite a Clean Air Act with mechanisms to address transboundary haze .
 Follow the money
 Being linked to fires is not the same as being proven responsible, and further audits and evidence are needed. But if these companies’ involvement can be confirmed, the next question is who owns and funds them. Companies have shareholders and lenders, and many of those are institutions ordinary people pay into: pension funds, unit trusts, and banks. That is why the haze is also a question about finance.
 Why this connects to coal
 The same fine particles we tracked all season, PM2.5, are released by coal plants every day, and coal PM2.5 carries more than twice the mortality risk of PM2.5 from other sources. Coal now generates 43% of Malaysia’s electricity , up from 6% in 2000.
 We’ve asked banks about this before. In 2020, a campaign organised between Greenpeace Indoneisa & Malaysia as well as several allies, ran a full-page ad, “CIMB is funding a Hotter Earth” , citing data that CIMB, Maybank and RHB provided US$4.9 billion to coal between 2010 and 2019. CIMB then committed to phase out coal financing by 2040 . In 2021 we pressed Maybank over its coal power financing , and it stopped financing new coal . But as our open letter notes, these pledges cover new coal, not existing financing, which continues.
 What we’re asking for
 1. Screen for harm, and act when it continues Regulators and banks should proactively conduct real ethical screening and due diligence on who they finance, from before a deal is signed to the day it ends. Labels and reports mean little if the harm continues. Islamic finance calls for preventing harm, protecting life and serving the public good. These principles should also extend to conventional finance.
 2. Protect health and environment Financing should ensure no negative health and environmental impacts will occur as a result of operational activities. In the case of transboundary haze, agricultural activities should not burn peatlands. It should also fund the rehabilitation of scarred and degraded peatlands: 97 to 99% of burned areas in Indonesia were never restored .
 3. Plan to protect people Financed projects should come with preventive plans for public health, so their operations do not endanger lives. Workers and communities affected should be supported, not left behind.
 4. For coal, exit ASAP A company earning 5% of its income from tobacco fails Malaysia’s Shariah screen , while one earning all of its income from coal can pass. Coal should be classed as harmful too. Banks should publish a dated exit from all coal finance by 2035, existing financing included, instead of waiting for contracts to expire, and report their coal exposure in ringgit every year.   
 Read the full open letter for more detailed information.
